name_en: Australian Black Tea (Daintree and Atherton Tablelands)
cultivar: Assamica-type seedling bushes and clones descended from the nineteenth-century Bingil Bay plantings and later introductions
processing: Machine-harvested leaf processed as CTC or fine-cut orthodox black tea: withered, cut or rolled, fully oxidised and fired; the Daintree estate makes an unblended single-origin tea, while the larger Tablelands producer blends for consistency.
harvest_season: Harvested year-round in the tropics, with the heaviest flushing in the wet season from December to April; there are no vintage distinctions.
appearance_dry: Small, dark, fine-cut leaf, granular in the CTC grades, with a plain sweet smell.
appearance_liquor: Bright reddish amber, clear, lighter than Assam.
taste_profile: Mild, smooth and low in tannin with a light malt and a faintly fruity, honeyed sweetness; it does not turn bitter when oversteeped, which is the selling point, and it takes milk without needing it.

brewing.notes: A Western pot or bag tea: boiling water, three to four minutes, milk optional. It is forgiving of long steeps and makes a clean iced tea.

vintage_note: Sold year-round by brand in bags and loose packs, never by harvest; the Daintree estate sells its own single-origin tea from the farm gate and online, and Nerada's supermarket packs are blended across the year. Use within a year or two of packing.
description:
Australia grows a little tea in the tropical north of Queensland, and two names cover most of it. Nerada, on the Atherton Tablelands inland from Cairns, is the big one, the country's largest producer and a supermarket brand for decades; the Daintree Tea Company, a family farm in the Daintree between the rainforest and the reef, is the small one, selling a single-origin tea from a business established in 1978. The industry's roots go back to the Cutten brothers, who planted tea at Bingil Bay in the 1880s; bushes that survived there were the starting point for Nerada's first plantings in 1958.

The climate is tropical, so the bushes are Assam types, the harvest runs all year with a wet-season peak, and the picking is done by machine. Processing is CTC or fine-cut black tea designed for the Australian cup of tea with milk. The Daintree farm says it grows without chemical sprays and sells its tea unblended, so that the pack is one place and one year's leaf.

In the cup, Australian black tea is mild, smooth and low in tannin, with a light malt and a faint fruity sweetness, and its great virtue is that it does not go bitter when forgotten in the pot. It is not a complex tea and does not claim to be; it is a friendly breakfast tea that is better plain than most CTC and takes milk gracefully.

It is sold by brand, not by harvest: Nerada in every Australian supermarket, Daintree from the farm, online and in Queensland shops. 'Australian grown' on a pack means something, since most tea sold in Australia is imported and blended; tea is also grown on a smaller scale in northern New South Wales (Madura, in the Tweed Valley), in Victoria's Alpine Valleys (mostly Japanese-style green tea) and in tiny amounts in Tasmania, but little of it travels far.

If you are passing through Far North Queensland, both estates can be visited; and the fair comparison at home is with a Kenyan or Argentine CTC, against which the Australian tea is softer and lighter.
history:
Commercial tea growing in Australia restarted in 1958, when Allan Maruff planted in the Nerada valley south of Cairns with seedlings from the Cutten brothers' old plantation at Bingil Bay; no commercial planting had happened since 1886. Australia's first commercial tea factory opened at Nerada in 1971.

Tea Estates of Australia, which had planted next door from 1969, bought Nerada in 1973 and sold the tea under that name, opening a larger factory at Glen Allyn near Malanda in 1991. Nerada remains the largest supplier of Australian-grown tea, with over 400 hectares and about 1,500 tonnes of black tea.

The Daintree Tea Company, established in 1978, is the small counterpart further north, and a few other growers work in New South Wales and Victoria.
